etymologies.etymologyHTML: The verb is from Middle English crien (13th century), from Old French crier, from Vulgar Latin *crītāre, generally thought to derive from Classical Latin quirītāre (Proto-West Germanic *krītan has also been suggested as a source). The noun corresponds to Middle English cry, crie, from Old French cri, a deverbal of crier.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To shed tears; to weep. Especially in anger or sadness

quote.citation: 2003, Sonic Team, Sonic Battle, Sega, published 2003, Game Boy Advance, level/area: Cream’s Story:
quote.text: - Emerl: “There’s nothing worse than making a girl cry!” That’s what Sonic said...

definitions.definition: (transitive) To utter loudly; to call out; to declare publicly.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:
quote.text: All, all, cry shame against ye, yet I'll speak.

quote.citation: 1678, John Bunyan, The Pilgrim’s Progress from This World, to That which is to Come: […], London:  […]  Nath[aniel] Ponder […], →OCLC, page 3:
quote.text: [T]he Man put his fingers in his Ears, and ran on crying, Life, Life, Eternal Life: [...]

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 27:46:
quote.text: And about the ninth hour, Jesus cried with a loud voice.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, figuratively) To forcefully attract attention or proclaim one’s presence.

quote.citation: 1941, Theodore Roethke, “Open House”, in Open House; republished in The Collected Poems of Theodore Roethke, 1975, →ISBN, page 3:
quote.text: My secrets cry aloud.I have no need for tongue.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To utter inarticulate sounds, as animals do.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalms 147:9:

1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: In a cowslip's bell I lie / There I couch when owls do cry.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to do something, or bring to some state, by crying or weeping.
Hence, to publish the banns of, as for marriage.

quote.citation: 1845, Sylvester Judd, Margaret: A Tale of the Real and the Ideal, Blight and Bloom; Including Sketches of a Place Not Before Described, Called Mons Christi:
quote.text: I should not be surprised if they were cried in church next Sabbath.

definitions.definition: To make oral and public proclamation of; to notify or advertise by outcry, especially things lost or found, goods to be sold, auctioned, etc.

quote.citation: 1652, Richard Crashaw, The Beginning of Heliodorus:
quote.text: Love is lost, and thus she cries him.

quote.citation: 1966 March, Thomas Pynchon, chapter 6, in The Crying of Lot 49, New York, N.Y.: Bantam Books, published November 1976, →ISBN, page 137:
quote.text: “We're in luck. Loren Passerine, the finest auctioneer in the West, will be crying today.” “Will be what?” “We say an auctioneer ‘cries’ a sale,” Cohen said.

quote.citation: 1976, Stan Rogers (lyrics and music), “Barrett's Privateers”, in Fogarty's Cove:
quote.text: Oh, Elcid Barrett cried the town / (How I wish I was in Sherbrooke now!) / For twenty brave men, all fishermen, who / Would make for him the Antelope's crew.

definitions.definition: A shedding of tears; the act of crying.

quote.citation: 1812, Alexander Chalmers, The General Biographical Dictionary:
quote.text: His pupil, Maimonides, that he might not be under the necessity of violating the laws of friendship and gratitude, by joining the general cry against Averroes, left Corduba.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “A Midsommer Nights Dreame”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: A cry more tunable / Was never hollaed to, nor cheered with horn.

quote.citation: 1667, Milton, Paradise Lost, Book II, in Edward Hawkins, The Poetical Works of John Milton: With Notes of Various Authors, Vol. I, W. Baxter, J. Parker, G. B. Whittaker (publs., 1824) pages 124 to 126, lines 648 to 659.
quote.text: […]  Before the gates there sat / On either side a formidable shape; / The one seem’d woman to the waste, and fair, / But ended foul in many a scaly fold / Voluminous and vast, a serpent arm’d / With mortal sting: about her middle round / A cry of hell-hounds never ceasing bark’d / With wide Cerberean mouths full loud and rung / A hideous peal; yet, when they list,would creep, / If ought disturb'd their noise, into her womb, / and kennel there, yet there still bark’d and howl’d, / Within unseen.  […]

definitions.definition: (by extension, obsolete, derogatory) A pack or company of people.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: Would not this  […]  get me a fellowship in a cry of players?

definitions.definition: (of an animal) A typical sound made by the species in question.

quote.citation: 1886, Peter Christen Asbjørnsen, translated by H.L. Brækstad, Folk and Fairy Tales, page 86:
quote.text: But the shrill wild cry of the heron overpowered the cries of all the other birds, whom it seemed to terrify; they were silent the moment they heard it, and a silence followed which made the interruption doubly unpleasant.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: The cry goes that you shall marry her.
